In most school-choice settings using a Deferred Acceptance (DA)-style mechanism, truthful reporting of preferences is a dominant strategy — misrepresenting preferences cannot improve your outcome and could only hurt you. 

Looking at my priorities: I have top priority (1) at both w and y, and lower priority (2) at x and z. My true preference order is x > y > w > z.

Since most other applicants prefer y > x > w > z, there will be heavy competition for y from students who also want it most. However, I have priority 1 at y, so I'm still well-positioned there regardless of demand. For x, I have priority 2, which is weaker, but it's my top choice — under DA, ranking it first still gives me the best chance the mechanism allows, since strategic demotion never helps under truthful mechanisms.

Given the incentive compatibility of standard DA-based assignment systems, the best strategy is simply to submit my true preference ordering without trying to game priorities.

This is a school-assignment matching setting where schools have priorities and students submit preference rankings. In the standard mechanism used for such problems (student-proposing deferred acceptance / Gale-Shapley), truthful reporting of one's own preference ordering is a dominant strategy — misrepresenting preferences cannot improve the outcome and can only hurt.

My true preferences are w > x > y > z. Looking at my priorities: I have top priority (1) at x and z, and lower priority (2) at w and y. Since most other applicants rank y first and x second, competition for y and x will be intense among those applicants, but my priority position at x (rank 1) gives me a strong chance there regardless of competition. My priority at w (rank 2) is not top, but since most applicants prefer y and x over w, fewer competitors will target w, improving my real chances there despite the lower priority number.

Since the mechanism is strategy-proof under DA, I will simply submit my true preference order rather than trying to "game" the system, as truthful revelation guarantees my best achievable outcome given the mechanism's properties.
